faqs.question: Will a tutor come to our home in Al Quoz for IGCSE lessons?
faqs.answer: Not through IB Gram. We teach IGCSE one-to-one into Al Quoz homes over live video, and we do not send tutors to any UAE address; home visits are a service we run only in India. Other Dubai providers do offer them, at market rates of roughly AED 180 to 500 per hour with travel built in, according to Bestimate's 2026 cost table. The reason we work online is board specificity: your child sits either Cambridge 0580 or Edexcel 4MA1, and we would rather match the right paper than the nearest postcode.

faqs.question: Is the February and March exam series an option for a candidate in Al Quoz?
faqs.answer: No. For Cambridge, a Dubai candidate sits the June series, with November available as the resit route. The February and March series is offered to India only and is not available to a candidate sitting in Dubai, which is a mistake worth avoiding because it is a date a family could plan around. For Pearson Edexcel International GCSE, examinations run in May and June and again in November. Your school's exams officer handles entries and holds the zone-correct timetable, and Cambridge states explicitly that using the wrong zone timetable is the candidate's risk.

faqs.question: We just had a bad mock in Year 11. How many weeks do we realistically need?
faqs.answer: Eight weeks is the planning unit that works, with six to twelve focused sessions inside it. The first week should be diagnosis rather than teaching: a specialist reading the mock script can usually say whether the problem is content, technique or timing, and those need entirely different work. Weeks two to six teach the gap and then test it on timed papers, and week eight is a review where stopping is a legitimate outcome. Two weeks of intensive work before the papers rarely moves a grade.

faqs.question: Should my child sit Core or Extended in Al Quoz schools?
faqs.answer: Decide it with a timed past paper from the harder tier, taken today with no help. If the score sits near the bottom of that tier's range, you have a real decision about whether eight weeks closes the gap or whether the capped tier produces the better grade. Remember it reaches forward: a Core Mathematics entry does not position a student for A Level Mathematics or Higher Level Analysis and Approaches. The confirmation deadline belongs to the school, so ask the subject teacher when it falls.

faqs.question: Does it matter whether the tutor knows Cambridge or Edexcel specifically?
faqs.answer: It matters a great deal in Year 11 and barely at all in Year 9. The content overlaps heavily, but the papers do not: structure, mark allocation, tiering language and the way practical skills are examined all differ between Cambridge 0625 and Edexcel 4PH1. In an eight-week block built on past papers, a tutor learning the board on your time is a direct cost to your child. Ask any prospective tutor which code they teach, and treat hesitation as an answer.

faqs.question: If we budget one session a week for a term, what should we expect to spend?
faqs.answer: Monthly is the right unit for that question. Bestimate's 2026 estimates for one weekly hour run roughly AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 for a mid-range qualified tutor, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist examination-year support. Advertised packages in this market include AED 799 per month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions. Those are other providers' published figures as at October 2026; ours are discussed after the free trial.

faqs.question: My child knows the content but the marks are not arriving. What is going on?
faqs.answer: Almost always command terms and mark-scheme wording. Describe, explain, suggest and compare each demand a different response shape, and a correct fact delivered in the wrong shape scores nothing. The fix is mechanical and fast: take three previously marked answers, rewrite them against the published scheme wording, and repeat until the student can predict the mark before the tutor gives it. This is usually a four-session problem, not a term-long one, which is why diagnosis before booking matters.

faqs.question: Is there any point starting IGCSE tutoring in Year 10?
faqs.answer: It is the cheapest point in the whole two years, and the one most families skip. A Year 10 student shaky on algebraic manipulation is a six-session problem. The same student in February of Year 11 needs those six sessions plus repair of everything built on top of the gap since, which is how a sensible hourly rate turns into an unsustainable total. Year 10 also still has room for an honest tier conversation, which Year 11 often does not.

faqs.question: Can my child retake an IGCSE in November if June goes badly?
faqs.answer: Yes. Both Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel run a November series, and for a Dubai candidate that is the resit route. Planning a November attempt is different from first-attempt work because the diagnosis is far better: you have the actual script and the actual grade, so the two or three topics that cost the grade can be identified precisely. Entry is arranged by the school's exams officer, not by a tutoring provider, and should be discussed as soon as results arrive.

faqs.question: How do Arabic and Islamic Education fit around a full IGCSE timetable?
faqs.answer: They sit on top of it. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools whatever the licensed curriculum, and KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, prohibiting combined classes because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Content is tightly controlled, with different or additional material needing prior Ministry of Education permission, so support works within the school's own material rather than around it.

faqs.question: A website told us six IGCSE passes are required in the UAE. Is that right?
faqs.answer: No. The published figure is five, not six. The published British-track rule requires five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no less than grade E or grade 3, plus either one subject at Advanced Level at grade E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are excluded from the five. One competitor page currently ranking in this market says six, which would change what a family makes their child sit, so verify the current rule on moe.gov.ae before planning around either number.

faqs.question: Can sessions run through the summer and during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes to both, and the summer is often the most productive block of the year for an Al Quoz family because term-time evenings are crowded and holiday mornings are not. Nothing is tied to a Dubai address, so lessons continue while the family travels, with the slot moved to a time that works in both zones. During Ramadan sessions commonly shift to post-Iftar timing, agreed with the tutor rather than imposed by a timetable.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover Maths and Physics for the same student?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is worth asking, because a single tutor across two related subjects reduces scheduling friction and the overlap in skills is real: a student who cannot rearrange an equation struggles in both. But the test is still board-and-component specific competence in each subject separately. If the candidate is strong in 0580 Mathematics and vague about 0625 Physics paper structure, two specialists serve the student better than one convenient diary.

faqs.question: What happens at the end of the eight weeks?
faqs.answer: A review against the next assessment, and a genuine recommendation. If the component is fixed, the right answer is to stop, and we will say so rather than converting the block into a standing weekly session. If a second component now looks like the priority, that is a new short block with its own diagnosis. The failure mode this avoids is the one that costs families most in this market: an open-ended arrangement that nobody examines until the series has already happened.

intro.heading: A tutoring plan that ignores the school run does not survive the term
paragraphs: Families in Al Quoz 4 book tutoring and then lose it to logistics. The arrangement looks sensible in September: two sessions a week, a reasonable rate, a tutor who seemed capable. By late October one session a week is being rescheduled, by November the student is tired at the start of every lesson, and by the spring the family concludes that tutoring did not work. What did not work was the timetable, and it was predictable from the first week.

Al Quoz 4 is part of the Al Quoz district, a mixed area along Al Khail Road where residential blocks sit alongside industrial and warehouse zones, between the Al Barsha South and Dubai Hills developments on one side and the Business Bay and Downtown corridor on the other. It has no single catchment school. Children here travel in several directions, by bus and by car, and arrival times vary by forty minutes or more between households on the same street depending on which school they attend.

That variation is why generic advice fails. A 16:30 session is realistic for a student at an Al Quoz school and impossible for one travelling back from Dubai Sports City. A ninety-minute session is fine on a Saturday morning and wasted on a Tuesday after a long bus route. A two-sessions-a-week plan is sustainable if both land in the right window and unsustainable if one of them sits ten minutes too early. None of that is about teaching quality and all of it determines the outcome.

So this page is built around the school run. It sets out the school clusters this area feeds, with the direction, the typical end of the day and the realistic session start for each. It maps the afternoon hour by hour. It says what can honestly fit into a week by year group. And it answers the home-tutor question specifically for this commute rather than in the abstract.

On that question we are direct, because the search deserves a straight answer. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. We teach one-to-one, online, over live video, in Gulf Standard Time. For this area the honest argument is partly cost and mostly reliability: a session that depends on nobody driving along Al Khail Road at the worst hour of the day is a session that happens.

Published Dubai figures put an in-home visit at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel inside the fee, against roughly AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor working online and AED 45 to 150 at the budget end. Those come from provider pages and the Bestimate Dubai rate table. They are the market and not our price list, and they are on this page because most pages competing for this search publish no figure at all.

sections.heading: Which schools this neighbourhood feeds, and what time the day actually ends
paragraphs: Al Quoz 4 does not have a catchment school, and that single fact explains most of the scheduling difficulty families here report. Children travel in at least four directions: to the Al Quoz schools a short distance away, across Al Khail Road to Al Khail Heights and Dubai Hills, south-west to Al Barsha South, and in some cases out along the Dubailand belt to Motor City or Sports City or across Sheikh Zayed Road to Al Safa. Those journeys differ by half an hour or more.

The published school finish time is not the number to plan from. What matters is when the student walks through the door, which is the finish time plus the bus route plus whatever the traffic does on that corridor at that hour. Al Khail Road and Sheikh Zayed Road both carry heavy afternoon loads, and a bus that collects from several stops adds time that no timetable shows. Families consistently underestimate this by twenty to thirty minutes when they book a tutor.

Then add the human part: food, a change of clothes, and the ten minutes a teenager needs before being useful. Forty minutes after arrival is a realistic floor, not a generous allowance. A session booked at the arrival time plus twenty minutes will be attended with a sandwich in hand and will produce roughly half of what the same hour produces an hour later, which is a poor use of a paid session.

The table below sets out the clusters this area feeds with their direction, the typical end of the day and the session start we would actually recommend. It is drawn from how families here describe their afternoons rather than from published timetables, and it is deliberately conservative, because a slot that works on a good day and fails on a bad one costs more in rescheduled lessons than it saves in convenience.

sections.heading: The afternoon hour by hour, and what genuinely fits
paragraphs: It helps to look at the afternoon as a sequence of windows with different properties rather than as a block of free time. The hour immediately after arrival is not usable for teaching and attempts to use it are the main source of rescheduled sessions. The window from roughly 17:00 is where sustained work is possible for most students here. After about 19:30 retention falls away and a session becomes attendance rather than learning.

That gives most households a working window of about two to two and a half hours on a weekday, inside which school homework, activities, family time and any tutoring all have to fit. Treating a tutoring session as an addition to that window rather than a claim on it is how plans fail. One hour taken deliberately, at a consistent time, leaves the rest intact. Two hours taken on the same evening does not, and the second hour is the one that gets cancelled.

This is also why one reliable session a week usually outperforms two unreliable ones. An eight-week block with two sessions a week is sixteen appointments, and what the family actually buys is the number that take place. If two a month are lost to a slot that was always slightly too early, a quarter of the block has gone, and that loss is larger than any plausible difference between two competent tutors.

The table maps the afternoon with what suits each window. Use it to choose a slot before choosing a tutor, which is the opposite of the usual order and produces better results. A good tutor at the wrong hour is a worse purchase than a solid tutor at the right one.

sections.heading: Al Quoz 4's particular geography, and why it matters to a tutoring plan
paragraphs: Al Quoz is an unusual district by Dubai standards: a working area where residential blocks, warehouses, workshops and galleries sit beside one another along Al Khail Road, with the newer master-planned communities on one side and the Business Bay and Downtown corridor on the other. For a family it is practical and well connected rather than scenic, and it is noticeably more affordable than the areas immediately around it.

Two features of that geography affect a tutoring arrangement directly. The first is that the area is served by major roads rather than by a dense local network, so journeys are fast when the roads are clear and slow when they are not, with little in between. That makes afternoon arrival times bimodal rather than average: a route is either twenty minutes or forty, and families plan for the first and experience the second.

The second is that there is no school at the centre of the community, so there is no shared rhythm. In a neighbourhood with a school in it, everyone's children get home at roughly the same time and activities organise themselves around that. Here, two families on the same street can have students arriving half an hour apart, which means advice that works for a neighbour may not work for you. The only reliable input is your own child's actual arrival time, observed over a week.

Study space is the third consideration and it needs a short conversation rather than being left to chance. Apartments here are practical rather than large, and the study surface is usually shared. Headphones are equipment rather than a luxury, a hard surface matters more than a dedicated room, and squared paper, a ruler and the student's own calculator rather than a phone should be ready before the first session. The camera goes on the page, because that is where the diagnosis happens.

sections.heading: Both boards are in use nearby, so confirm the code first
paragraphs: The schools this area feeds include both Cambridge and Pearson centres, and some schools use different boards for different subjects within the same year group. That makes the syllabus code the first thing to establish and the most common thing nobody checks. A student revising the wrong board's past papers is doing genuine work in a dialect that will not be spoken in the examination hall, and it is entirely preventable with one email.

In mathematics the practical difference is large. Cambridge 0580 sits two papers with one taken without a calculator, so non-calculator fluency, exact form and notation carry real weight. Pearson 4MA1 sits two equally weighted papers with a calculator allowed throughout, which shifts the risk to rounding, accuracy and interpreting the display. Cambridge 0607 is the graphic-display-calculator syllabus with an investigation element. Each has a separate past-paper library.

In the sciences the difference is in paper structure and in how practical skills are examined. Cambridge separate sciences assess practical skills either through a practical test or a written alternative-to-practical paper, and most international centres use the written route. Pearson examines practical knowledge inside its written papers. Cambridge tiers its separate sciences into Core and Extended with a capped ceiling on Core; Pearson's separate sciences are untiered.

The table sets out what to confirm with the examinations officer and what each answer changes. One email covering all of it takes two minutes to write and removes the single largest source of wasted revision time in this qualification. It is also the question most tutors should ask you first; if nobody has, that is worth noticing.

sections.heading: What honestly fits into a week here, by year group
paragraphs: A sensible plan starts from how much time exists rather than from how much support would be ideal. For a Year 7 to 9 student in this area the day usually ends earlier, activity commitments are lighter and one weekly session fits comfortably, with a second only if the household genuinely wants it. Shorter sessions work better at this age in any case, so forty-five minutes at a consistent time is often the right arrangement.

For a Year 10 student the week has more content in it and the journey has not changed, so one weekly session plus set work between is the realistic ceiling for most households. The temptation is to add a second subject, and it is usually better resisted in favour of choosing the single subject that gives the widest benefit. In practice that is frequently mathematics, because the same weaknesses that cost marks there also damage the sciences.

For a Year 11 student the week is fullest and the tutoring demand is highest, which is the central tension in this subject. Two sessions a week is achievable in the final term if one of them sits on a weekend morning. Two weekday evening sessions is not, for most students travelling out of this area, and attempting it produces the pattern where the second session is routinely cancelled and the family concludes that tutoring failed.

The honest planning rule is to count backwards from the available windows rather than forwards from the desired number of hours, and to subtract the school and public holidays before agreeing a session count. An eight-week block containing a holiday week and a school activity week is six weeks of teaching being sold as eight, and saying so in advance is the difference between a plan and a hopeful schedule.

sections.heading: The home-tutor question, answered for this specific commute
paragraphs: The search that brought you here asks about a home tutor, so here is the direct answer for this area rather than a general argument. An in-home arrangement in Al Quoz 4 requires a tutor to drive to you along Al Khail Road or Sheikh Zayed Road in the late afternoon, and to do it reliably every week for a term. Published Dubai rates put that at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel inside the fee, against roughly AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor working online.

The premium is a logistics charge rather than a quality one. There is no mechanism by which driving to Al Quoz improves somebody's grasp of Extended 0580 or 4CH1. What it buys is presence in the room, which has genuine value for a younger child or a student who will not stay on task alone, and we would not pretend otherwise. What it costs is selection: the tutor pool narrows to those willing to make that journey at that hour, which for a specific requirement is a short list.

It also costs reliability, and this is the point that matters most in an area with these road patterns. A tutor arriving fifteen minutes late has consumed a quarter of an hour that was paid for in full. A tutor who cannot come at all removes a week from a plan with no spare weeks in it. Over an eight-week block that is a material loss and it is larger than any plausible difference in teaching quality between two competent people.

IB Gram does not sell home visits anywhere in the UAE, so this is not a comparison we can be neutral about, and we have tried to state the in-home case fairly rather than straw-man it. Where a child is young or needs an adult beside them, an in-room arrangement is a reasonable buy and we are not the right provider. Where the requirement is a specific syllabus in a finite number of weeks, the slot that survives the term and the tutor who has taught the code are what decide the outcome.

sections.heading: Ramadan, holidays and two different term calendars
paragraphs: Three calendar features complicate a plan in this area more than elsewhere. The first is Ramadan, when Dubai schools adjust their hours for several weeks. The arrangement that works is fewer and shorter sessions moved to the late morning or the post-Iftar window, with lighter work set between them, agreed before the month begins rather than improvised through it. For a Year 11 student those weeks frequently sit close to a mock series.

The second is that the schools this area feeds do not share a calendar. A household with one child at an Al Quoz school and another at a school in Al Barsha South or Motor City can have two different half-term weeks, two different mock windows and two different activity calendars. Planning around the busier child's calendar rather than pretending both are flexible avoids the usual outcome, which is that the quieter child's sessions are the ones cancelled.

The third is the long summer and the winter break, both of which sit immediately before high-stakes terms and both of which are undervalued. Short daily sessions across two or three weeks of a holiday hold better than one weekly session during term, because the spacing is tighter and nothing competes. For families travelling out of Dubai an online arrangement simply follows them, which is the one scheduling advantage of the format that nobody disputes.

On the examination calendar itself: Cambridge IGCSE runs in June and November, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November. Those are the windows open to a UAE candidate. The Cambridge February and March series is offered to India only. Cambridge also allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states it is essential to use the correct timetable version for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong one. Ask the school for your version and keep it.

sections.heading: Permits, honest limits and what to verify yourself
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is lawful and regulated by permit, which is worth knowing in an area where informal home tuition is widely available. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is issued through MoHRE, granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, university students, and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time, with the application made through its smart app, website and e-services system.

Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so no amount appears on this page; a figure circulating online could not be verified and publishing it would be guesswork presented as fact. Asking a tutor about their permit is an ordinary question with an ordinary answer. We would also advise against any arrangement involving your child's own schoolteacher, which the permit's code of conduct and reported regulatory rules both point away from.

IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from Cambridge, Pearson, the International Baccalaureate, KHDA, ADEK, SPEA or the Ministry of Education, and no page here will claim one. We operate no office, centre or branch in the UAE, we run no home visits anywhere in the Emirates, we do not enter candidates for examinations, and we do not perform Ministry equivalency. A tutoring operation with premises in Dubai requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute; we hold none because we have no premises.

On materials and figures: we reference and link official syllabus, specimen and timetable documents rather than reproducing them, and we do not supply board-owned papers, mark schemes or grade-boundary tables as downloads. Your child's school has legitimate access through its own subscriptions. Every number on this page carries a source, and we publish no success rates, satisfaction scores or star ratings. Private schools in Dubai are overseen by KHDA, described on u.ae as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate, and its inspection reports live on its own site.

faqs.question: What time should an IGCSE session start for a student living in Al Quoz 4?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on which school they attend, because this area has no catchment school and journeys differ by half an hour or more. Students at Al Quoz schools are often home by 15:45 and can manage 16:30. Students crossing Al Khail Road to Dubai Hills or travelling to Al Barsha South are home a little after 16:00, so 17:00 is sensible. Students going out to Motor City or Sports City need 17:30 or later. Observe the actual arrival time for a week, then add forty minutes.

faqs.question: Will IB Gram send a tutor to our home in Al Quoz 4?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; sending a tutor to a family address is a service we run only in India. Lessons here are one-to-one online over live video in Gulf Standard Time. For this area the argument is mostly reliability: an in-home arrangement needs somebody to drive Al Khail Road or Sheikh Zayed Road in the late afternoon every week for a term, and a tutor arriving fifteen minutes late has consumed a quarter of an hour you paid for in full.

faqs.question: For a long bus route from Al Quoz 4, is one weekly session better than two?
faqs.answer: For most students travelling out of this area, one reliable weekly session plus set work is better than two sessions where one is routinely rescheduled. An eight-week block with two a week is sixteen appointments, and losing two a month to a slot that was always slightly too early removes a quarter of the block. If two are genuinely needed, put one of them on a weekend morning rather than on a second weekday evening, which is the arrangement that actually survives a term here.

faqs.question: Why is a weekend morning better than a weekday evening?
faqs.answer: Because nothing competes with it and the student has not just finished a journey. Weekday evenings in this area start late, carry school homework and activities, and leave a working window of about two hours into which everything has to fit. A weekend morning supports ninety minutes of real work, which is enough for a whole paper under timed conditions or a long practical-skills session. It is the most productive slot we offer and consistently the least requested, which is worth knowing.

faqs.question: Which school cluster does Al Quoz 4 actually feed?
faqs.answer: Several, which is the root of the scheduling difficulty. There are schools a short distance away in Al Quoz, newer provision across Al Khail Road in Al Khail Heights and Dubai Hills, a cluster in Al Barsha South, established schools across Sheikh Zayed Road in Al Safa, and longer routes out to Motor City and Dubai Sports City. Two families on the same street can therefore have students arriving home half an hour apart, which means advice that works for a neighbour may not work for you.

faqs.question: Our tutoring last year did not work. What usually goes wrong?
faqs.answer: In this area, more often the timetable than the teaching. A slot set from the school's finish time rather than the actual arrival, a ninety-minute session on a school night, two weekday evening sessions for a student with a long bus route, or a block whose session count ignored the holidays in it. Each of those produces the same pattern: steady rescheduling from about week four and a conclusion in the spring that tutoring failed. Fixing the slot usually fixes more than changing the tutor does.

faqs.question: How do we find out which board our child's school uses?
faqs.answer: Ask the examinations officer, and ask subject by subject, because schools near this area use both Cambridge and Pearson and sometimes different boards for different subjects within the same year group. In the same email ask for the maths code, the tier, whether sciences are separates or an award, how practical skills are examined, and which English qualification is on the entry. That one message removes the largest avoidable source of wasted revision time in this qualification.

faqs.question: What does in-home tutoring cost here compared with online?
faqs.answer: Published Dubai rates put an in-home one-to-one visit at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with the tutor's travel inside the fee, with monthly packages around AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour visits. A qualified subject tutor working online is quoted at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with budget options from about AED 45 and specialists from about AED 200 to 450 or more. Those come from published provider pages and the Bestimate Dubai rate table. The difference is almost entirely travel rather than teaching.

faqs.question: Is in-home tutoring ever the better option for a family here?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. For a younger child, presence in the room has genuine value that a screen does not fully replace, and the same applies to a student who will not stay on task without an adult beside them. We do not sell that format anywhere in the UAE, so we are not the right provider in those cases. Where the requirement is a specific syllabus in a finite number of weeks, the slot that survives the term and the tutor who has taught the code are what decide the outcome.

faqs.question: Which single subject should we fund if the budget is fixed?
faqs.answer: Usually the one a marked paper identifies rather than the one that feels hardest, and in practice that is often mathematics. The rearrangement, standard form and proportional reasoning that cost marks there also damage physics and chemistry calculations, so repairing it lifts more than one grade. Biology is more often a terminology and point-counting problem that a disciplined student can work on with less supervision once the method has been taught. Send one marked paper per subject and we will name the order.

faqs.question: Do holiday blocks work for a family in this area?
faqs.answer: Well, and better than term-time sessions for content repair. Short daily sessions across two or three weeks of a break hold more than one weekly session during term, because the spacing is tighter and nothing competes for the student's attention. The long Dubai summer and the winter break both sit immediately before high-stakes terms. Because sessions run online, a family travelling out of the UAE keeps the arrangement, which is the one scheduling advantage of the format that nobody argues with.

faqs.question: Can sessions be rearranged during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and we agree the change before the month begins rather than improvising through it. Dubai schools adjust their hours during Ramadan, and most families want fewer and shorter sessions rather than the same timetable pushed later. Late-morning slots suit students whose day has been compressed, and the post-Iftar window suits households that prefer the evening. We also lighten the work set between sessions. For a Year 11 student those weeks often sit close to a mock series, which is exactly why the shift is worth planning.

faqs.question: We have two children at two different schools. How do we plan around that?
faqs.answer: Around the busier child's calendar rather than pretending both are flexible. The schools this area feeds do not share half-terms, mock windows or activity weeks, so a household can face two different pressure periods in the same month. In practice the quieter child's sessions are the ones that get cancelled when the two collide. Put both calendars on one page in September, pick the weeks where only one child is under pressure, and accept that one of them will need a holiday block rather than a term-time slot.

faqs.question: Does a tutor working in Al Quoz need a UAE permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated through the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published, so treat any amount you read as unverified. Asking about the permit is a reasonable question in any arrangement.

intro.heading: Which syllabus is your child actually sitting?
paragraphs: An Al Qusais parent looking for an IGCSE home tutor usually has one piece of information: a subject name and a worried teacher. What they almost never have, because the school rarely volunteers it, is the syllabus code. That four-digit number decides nearly everything a tutor should be doing. Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics is 0580 and tiers into Core and Extended. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics Specification A is 4MA1 and tiers into Foundation and Higher. The question styles differ, the formula sheets differ, and the grade a given raw mark produces differs.

The same split runs through the sciences. Cambridge Physics is 0625, Chemistry 0620 and Biology 0610, each with an alternative-to-practical option alongside the practical paper. Pearson's equivalents are 4PH1, 4CH1 and 4BI1, with practical skills assessed inside the written papers instead. A tutor who has spent five years on Cambridge 0620 past papers and is handed a 4CH1 student will teach good chemistry and miss the paper technique that converts it into marks.

So the honest starting point for this page is not a sales pitch. It is an instruction: look at your child's exam entry confirmation, or email the head of year, and get the codes. Then find a tutor who teaches those codes. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in Dubai; home visits are something we run only in India. For families in Al Qusais, every lesson is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, which is precisely what makes a code-level match possible rather than aspirational.

Dubai's private-school market is the right size for this to matter. The emirate had 227 private schools and 387,441 pupils in 2024-25 across seventeen curricula, with the UK curriculum the largest at 37% of enrolment and the Indian curriculum next at 26%, according to the Dubai Media Office. Dubai's 2026-27 intake adds seven more private schools, four of them UK curriculum, creating 16,846 new places. A large British-curriculum cohort spread across two examination boards is exactly the situation in which a generic tutor sounds entirely plausible on a phone call and then underperforms for a full term. Nothing in the conversation reveals the mismatch, because the subject name is the same on both specifications and only the paper shows the difference.

This page covers the board question, the Core and Extended decision and the grade ceiling it imposes, how practical assessment works when lessons happen on screen, what the Dubai market charges by month rather than by hour, which schools around Al Qusais run IGCSE and in which year, the November series as a resit route, and the Ministry of Education's five-subject equivalency rule that one ranking competitor currently states incorrectly. Each of those is something a parent can settle in a single evening, and none of it requires buying anything first.

Cambridge grades 9 to 1 on most syllabuses with A* to G retained on some, and tiers several subjects into Core and Extended. Pearson grades 9 to 1 and tiers maths into Foundation and Higher. Coursework exists on a minority of subjects only.

dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-al-qusais.subjectsIntro: These are the IGCSE subjects Dubai families most often ask about, with the Cambridge code where one applies. Each note says what the paper actually rewards, because that is the difference between knowing content and scoring it.

subjects.name: Mathematics (0580 Cambridge / 4MA1 Pearson)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, or Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: Extended and Higher tier questions chain several steps, so a method error in line one loses the lot. Cambridge Extended students most often lose marks on functions, vectors and compound interest. Pearson Higher papers lean harder on structured problem-solving with fewer scaffolded steps.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics (0606)
subjects.description: Taken alongside 0580 by stronger sets as a bridge to A Level. Introduces calculus, logarithms and trigonometric identities early. Students who cope with Extended and then struggle here are usually short on algebraic fluency rather than on the new topics.

subjects.name: Physics (0625 Cambridge / 4PH1 Pearson)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
subjects.description: Electricity and waves are where Extended grades separate. Cambridge offers a practical paper or the alternative-to-practical, while Pearson assesses practical skills inside the written papers. Marks go missing in unit conversion and in graph work that is drawn rather than interpreted.

subjects.name: Chemistry (0620 Cambridge / 4CH1 Pearson)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
subjects.description: Moles calculations and organic chemistry decide the top grades. The qualitative analysis section rewards memorised observations, which is unusual in this subject and often untaught. Balanced equations with state symbols are the cheapest marks most candidates leave behind.

subjects.name: Biology (0610 Cambridge / 4BI1 Pearson)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
subjects.description: Volume is the problem, not difficulty. Transport in plants, genetics and homeostasis carry most of the lost marks. The command terms matter: describe, explain and compare each want a different shape of answer, and candidates routinely give the same shape to all three.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (0510 / 0511)
subjects.description: Reading comprehension and the two writing tasks dominate the grade. Registers are the trap: a candidate who writes an email in essay prose loses marks they never see. Summary writing to a word limit is a learnable technique and the fastest grade movement available in this subject.

subjects.name: First Language English (0500 / 0990)
subjects.description: Directed writing and the reading passages reward control rather than vocabulary. Most lost marks come from candidates narrating a passage instead of analysing how its language works. The timing split between reading and writing is as important as the content knowledge.

subjects.name: Business Studies (0450)
subjects.description: Case-study driven, with application marks that require naming the business in the answer rather than discussing business in general. Break-even, cash flow and the marketing mix are the calculation and framework points where candidates can bank marks reliably.

subjects.name: Economics (0455)
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy carries the structured questions. Candidates lose evaluation marks by listing advantages and disadvantages without reaching a judgement. Elasticity and the multiplier are the two topics most often half-learned and then half-applied under time pressure.

subjects.name: Computer Science (0478)
subjects.description: Paper 1 theory rewards precise terminology on data representation and networks. Paper 2 is algorithm design and trace tables, where candidates who can code informally still lose marks for pseudocode that does not follow the published conventions.

sections.heading: Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel? Settle this before anything else
paragraphs: Dubai schools split between Cambridge International and Pearson Edexcel, and some run both across different subjects. Neither is harder in any meaningful general sense, but they assess differently enough that a tutor needs to know which one is in play. Ask the school for the syllabus or specification codes on your child's entry. A single email answers it.

Cambridge tiers several subjects. In Mathematics 0580, Core candidates sit papers assessing a reduced content list with a grade ceiling, and Extended candidates sit the full list. The sciences follow the same pattern. Pearson's International GCSE Mathematics Specification A, 4MA1, tiers into Foundation and Higher instead, and its science specifications are single tier with practical skills tested inside the written papers rather than in a separate practical or alternative paper.

The practical consequence for tutoring is paper technique. Cambridge structured questions tend to scaffold a long problem into labelled parts, which rewards candidates who work methodically through given steps. Pearson Higher papers more often present a problem whole and expect the candidate to choose the route. A student who is strong at one and weak at the other is not short of knowledge; they are short of practice in the format they will actually meet.

There is one more reason to confirm the board early. Resit and entry arrangements differ, and so do the timetables. Cambridge runs a June series and a November series, with every centre allocated to one of six administrative zones, and Cambridge states that it is essential to use the correct zone timetable and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. Pearson International GCSE runs May/June and November. Neither board's February or March arrangements apply to UAE candidates; that series is offered to India only.

sections.heading: Core or Extended: the grade ceiling nobody mentions at parents' evening
paragraphs: Tiering is the most consequential decision in the IGCSE years and the one families understand least. On a tiered Cambridge subject, a Core entry covers less content and caps the grade available. An Extended entry covers the full content and opens the top grades but makes a low grade possible where Core would have been safer. Pearson's Foundation and Higher split in 4MA1 works the same way.

Schools make this decision on internal evidence, usually in Year 10 or early Year 11, and they make it conservatively because a cohort of candidates entered above their level damages a school's results profile. That incentive is not wrong, but it is not identical to your child's interest. A student on the boundary who is entered Core in November of Year 10 and then improves sharply has lost the top grades before the improvement happened.

This is where tutoring in Year 10 earns its money, and it is a narrow, specific job. The task is to generate evidence: a run of Extended-tier past-paper questions marked honestly, so that the conversation with the school is about marks rather than impressions. If the evidence says Core, Core is the right answer and a tutor should say so. A confident Core grade 5 is worth more than a scattered Extended grade 4.

The same logic applies in reverse for subjects a child will not continue. A student heading for A Level Chemistry and Maths does not need to chase the top grade in nine subjects. Prioritising the four or five that function as gates, and accepting solid grades elsewhere, is the cheapest tutoring plan available and the one most Al Qusais families arrive at anyway, usually a year later than they should have.

sections.heading: How science practicals work when lessons happen on screen
paragraphs: This is the most common objection from parents in this district, and it deserves a straight answer rather than reassurance. Your child's practical work happens at school, in the school laboratory, supervised by the school. That does not change and no tutor should be offering to replace it. What a tutor works on is the part of practical assessment that is actually examined on paper.

In Cambridge sciences, candidates sit either a practical test or the alternative-to-practical paper, and in both cases a large share of the marks come from things that can be taught at a desk: reading a scale to the correct precision, tabulating results with consistent significant figures, plotting a graph with sensible axes, drawing a line of best fit rather than joining dots, identifying the independent and controlled variables, and spotting the anomalous reading. Pearson embeds the same skills inside its written papers.

Those skills are lost in predictable places. Candidates write a conclusion that restates the data instead of answering the question. They describe a precaution as a safety point when the mark is for accuracy. They identify a source of error without saying what effect it has on the result. None of this requires a laboratory to fix. It requires a tutor with the mark scheme and a student who has to explain their reasoning out loud.

Where a screen genuinely helps is in the marking. A past-paper graph photographed and annotated live, with the mark scheme beside it, shows a student exactly where the two marks went. The annotated version stays in the shared session notes, so in April the student revises from their own January errors rather than from a textbook they have already read twice.

sections.heading: What IGCSE support costs around Al Qusais, read as a monthly figure
paragraphs: Parents budget monthly, so take the market that way first. Bestimate's Dubai estimates for weekly one-hour sessions run roughly AED 240 to 600 a month at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support. Packages advertised in this market include around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home visits. The jump between those two package prices is the travel, not the teaching.

Converted to hours, the ladder starts low. EdFlik advertises from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from about AED 33 to 52 at entry level, which in practice buys homework supervision. Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 an hour, TutorChase quotes around AED 270, and Bestimate's rate table puts specialist IGCSE, IB and A-Level work at AED 200 to 450 and above. In-home visits are quoted at AED 180 to 350 by Bestimate, with independent home tutors advertising AED 200 to 500.

Where does the money get wasted around here? Three places, repeatedly. Buying two-hour sessions for a Year 10 student who loses attention after fifty minutes. Paying a specialist rate for homework supervision that a cheaper tutor would do as well. And paying a travel premium for a tutor whose subject match is weaker than the online alternative at the same price. Each of those is avoidable with one question asked before the first invoice.

These figures are what other providers in this market publish, read in October 2026. They are not IB Gram's prices and should not be read as a quote. Set against them is a piece of context worth having: KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private-school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year, under an economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion. For many Al Qusais households, a frozen fee bill is what makes a tutoring line affordable at all.

sections.heading: Which schools near Al Qusais run IGCSE, and when the decisions get made
paragraphs: Al Qusais and the districts around it carry a mix of British-curriculum schools entering candidates for Cambridge or Pearson, Indian-curriculum schools that enter IGCSE subjects alongside their main board, and schools that run a different programme to Year 9 before switching. For a parent, the practical question is not which school is best but which board that school uses and when it fixes option blocks.

Most schools in this corridor set Year 10 option blocks towards the end of Year 9, in the spring term. That timing is the hinge. A child who wants to keep triple science or add Additional Mathematics 0606 needs the evidence in hand before those forms are collected, which means autumn of Year 9 is when tutoring changes what is possible rather than merely improving a grade.

Dubai private schools are regulated by KHDA, which is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate and publishes annual inspection ratings on a six-band scale from Outstanding to Very Weak. An inspection report is worth reading for a specific reason: the subject commentary often names where attainment in a particular group is weaker than the school's overall band, which tells a parent more than the headline rating does.

Families in Al Nahda, on the Dubai-Sharjah boundary, should note that the regulator follows the school rather than the home. A Sharjah private school answers to the Sharjah Private Education Authority, which regulates private education in that emirate and also approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. A Dubai school answers to KHDA. In a household with children on both sides of the boundary, that is two different sets of inspection reports to read.

sections.heading: The November series as a resit route, and the deadline months before it
paragraphs: Resits are planned badly more often than any other part of the IGCSE year, because families think about the exam date and the exam date is the last thing that matters. What matters is the entry deadline, which falls months earlier, and whether the school is willing to enter the candidate at all.

Here is the sourced example. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs series in May/June and November. The November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. For the previous cycle, November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026, while June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026. So a candidate who gets a disappointing grade in late August and wants a November retake has roughly eight weeks of teaching time, and an entry decision that has to be made almost immediately.

Cambridge candidates in the UAE sit the June and November series. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam as a result of using the wrong one. Ask your school which zone it is in before you plan anything around a date. The February and March series is offered to India only and does not apply to candidates sitting in the UAE.

One further caution: Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, and dates can be revised. Always work from the live official timetable on the board's own site rather than from a restated date on a tutoring page, including this one. sections.heading: Five subjects at grade E: the equivalency rule stated correctly
paragraphs: Ministry of Education equivalency is the paperwork that converts a foreign school certificate into something a UAE university or employer can accept, and it is where families discover late that a subject choice made in Year 9 had a consequence. For the British track, the published requirement is that a student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade.

The detail that catches people is the exclusion. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects for the GCSE and IGCSE count. A student who takes Arabic and Islamic Education alongside four other IGCSEs has four counting subjects, not six. One competitor currently ranking for these queries states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects, which is not the published rule. Knowing the correct number is worth more to a family than any amount of tutoring marketing.

For the American track the same source sets out different conditions: English proficiency through a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and mathematics through at least 450 in the SAT Math test before applying. For the IB, no points threshold should be taken from any tutoring page, including this one, without being read on moe.gov.ae or confirmed with the attestation authority directly.

Two things follow. Equivalency is not something IB Gram performs, guarantees or accelerates, and tutoring is not required for it. What a tutor can do is make sure the five counting subjects are not the five being neglected, which is a subject-prioritisation conversation in Year 10 rather than an administrative one in Year 13. Verify your own case through the official channel; the rule above is published, but individual cases vary.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside the IGCSE timetable
paragraphs: Every Dubai private school teaches these subjects regardless of its licensed international curriculum, and families on the British curriculum routinely treat them as background noise until a report card says otherwise. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools, and KHDA required its arrangements to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April.

The organisation of these classes is prescribed rather than left to the school. KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and states that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, with the school's licensed-curriculum language used for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in Moral, Social and Cultural studies.

There are constraints on materials too, and they apply directly to tutoring. For the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited. Schools must also ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold the appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects. So tutoring in this area is support with the school's own prescribed material, not an alternative course, and any provider offering a parallel syllabus here is offering something that should not exist.

Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and KHDA advises that any mandatory-subject lesson should run at least 25 minutes. For an Al Qusais family, the planning point is simple arithmetic: these subjects occupy real timetable hours alongside nine or ten IGCSE subjects, and a tutoring plan that assumes the week has more room than it does will be the first thing dropped.

process.title: Send us the syllabus codes
process.description: The subject, the board and the code: 0580 or 4MA1, 0620 or 4CH1. If you do not have them, the school's head of year will confirm them in one email. Everything after this step depends on getting it right, and it is the step most providers skip.

process.title: Tier and priority check
process.description: We look at which subjects are tiered, which are gates for the post-16 route your child wants, and which can safely be left at a solid grade. That usually reduces the tutoring question from nine subjects to two or three.

process.title: A trial lesson on current material
process.description: Your child works with the proposed tutor on a topic from this week's class, using papers from the correct board. You get a short written note on what the tutor found. If the match is wrong, we change it rather than defend it.

process.title: Weekly sessions timed to the school run
process.description: A fixed slot set against when your child actually gets home to Al Qusais, usually between 16:00 and 20:00 Gulf Standard Time. Same tutor each week, with a written summary after each session so you can see the plan moving.

process.title: Mock review and a spring reset
process.description: Mock papers are read as diagnostics rather than predictions: which command terms lost marks, which topics, which timing errors. The plan for the final term is rebuilt from that evidence rather than continuing on momentum.

whyPoints.title: Matched to the code, not the subject name
whyPoints.description: A 0625 tutor and a 4PH1 tutor are doing different jobs. We ask for the board and code before matching, because the paper technique that converts knowledge into marks is board-specific and that is where most lost marks sit.

whyPoints.title: Tier decisions made on evidence
whyPoints.description: Core or Extended, Foundation or Higher, is the most consequential call in these two years. We generate marked past-paper evidence so the conversation with the school is about marks rather than impressions, and we say when Core is the right answer.

whyPoints.title: Market rates published with sources
whyPoints.description: Every AED figure here is attributed to the provider or rate table that published it, with the month read. Nothing on this page is a quote from IB Gram; our own figure comes after a trial, against a known subject and session length.

whyPoints.title: Delivery stated before you ask
whyPoints.description: Lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai and runs no UAE centre. You know what you are buying before any money is discussed.

whyPoints.title: Exam dates taken from the boards
whyPoints.description: Session windows and results dates on this page come from Pearson's and Cambridge's own published material, with the source named. Boards revise provisional timetables, so we point to the live official timetable rather than asking you to trust a restated date.

whyPoints.title: Subject prioritisation instead of blanket cover
whyPoints.description: Nine subjects do not all need tutoring. We identify the ones that gate the post-16 route and the ones where a solid grade is enough, which usually cuts the cost of a plan before it starts rather than after.

faqs.question: How do I find out whether my child's school uses Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel for IGCSE?
faqs.answer: Ask the head of year or the examinations officer for the syllabus or specification codes on your child's entry, subject by subject. Cambridge codes are four digits, such as 0580 for Mathematics or 0620 for Chemistry. Pearson International GCSE codes begin with a digit and letters, such as 4MA1 or 4CH1. Some Dubai schools use both boards across different subjects, so one answer for the whole timetable is not safe. Tutoring without this information means working from the wrong past papers, which costs marks that have nothing to do with how well your child understands the subject.

faqs.question: Does it matter for my child which of the two maths specifications the school picked?
faqs.answer: Neither is harder in any general sense, but they reward different habits. Cambridge Extended structured questions usually break a long problem into labelled parts, so a methodical candidate who follows given steps does well. Pearson Higher papers more often present a problem whole and expect the candidate to choose the route themselves. A student strong on one format and weak on the other is short of practice rather than short of knowledge. That is exactly why a tutor needs the code before the first session rather than after the first mock.

faqs.question: My child has been put in for Core maths. Can that still be changed?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and the window is narrower than parents expect. Schools usually fix tier entries in Year 10 or early Year 11 on internal evidence, and they decide conservatively because over-entering a cohort damages their results profile. To change it you need marked evidence, not a conversation: a run of Extended-tier past-paper questions worked under timed conditions and marked against the published scheme. If that evidence says Core, Core is the honest answer. A secure Core grade is worth more than a scattered Extended one.

faqs.question: What does an IGCSE tutor around Al Qusais cost per month?
faqs.answer: Taking the market monthly, Bestimate's Dubai estimates for weekly one-hour sessions run about AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support. Advertised packages include roughly AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits. Those are other providers' published figures read in October 2026, not IB Gram's prices. Ours is quoted after a trial against your actual subject, level and session length.

faqs.question: How are science practicals assessed if the tutoring happens online?
faqs.answer: The practical work itself happens at school, in the school laboratory, and no tutor should offer to replace it. What is examined on paper is a set of desk-based skills: reading a scale to the right precision, tabulating with consistent significant figures, plotting and interpreting graphs, identifying variables, spotting anomalous readings and explaining the effect of an error on a result. Cambridge tests these in a practical test or the alternative-to-practical paper; Pearson embeds them in the written papers. All of it is teachable with a mark scheme and a shared screen.

faqs.question: Why does IB Gram not send a tutor to our building in Al Qusais?
faqs.answer: Because the travel requirement shrinks the tutor pool to whoever lives close enough to make the journey worthwhile, which in practice means a weaker subject match at a higher price. In-home visits in Dubai are quoted at AED 180 to 500 an hour against AED 150 to 300 for a qualified online tutor, and the difference is the journey rather than the teaching. Home visits are a service IB Gram runs only in India. For Al Qusais families every lesson is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time.

faqs.question: How many IGCSE subjects should we actually pay for tutoring in?
faqs.answer: Usually two or three, not nine. The subjects worth paying a specialist rate for are the ones that gate the next step: most Dubai schools set an entry grade for each A Level or IB subject, commonly a 6 or 7 for sciences and maths. Those are the gates. Subjects your child will not continue need a solid pass, not a top grade. Families who start by tutoring everything tend to stop tutoring everything by half term, having spent the budget on the wrong subjects.

faqs.question: When is the November series and is it worth retaking a subject?
faqs.answer: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs May/June and November, and the November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. Cambridge candidates in the UAE sit June and November. The constraint is time, not willingness: June 2026 results reached students on 20 August 2026, so a retake decision is made within days and leaves six to eight teaching weeks. It is worth it for one subject that gates a post-16 place. It is rarely worth it for three at once. Always check the live official timetable.

faqs.question: Is the February or March exam series available to candidates in Dubai?
faqs.answer: No. Cambridge offers the February and March series to India only. Candidates sitting in the UAE take the June and November series, and Pearson International GCSE runs May/June and November. This matters because incorrect advice on this point circulates widely, and a family that plans a retake around a February window discovers in December that no entry exists. Cambridge also allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and says it is essential to use the correct zone timetable, so ask your school which zone it sits in.

faqs.question: Will my child's Arabic grade be one of the five the Ministry counts?
faqs.answer: No, and this is the detail that catches families. For the British track, the published requirement is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. A student with Arabic, Islamic Education and four other IGCSEs therefore has four counting subjects. One competitor ranking for these queries states that UAE candidates need six IGCSE subjects, which is not the published rule. Verify your own case through the official Ministry channel.

faqs.question: Is it a problem if one of my child's subjects uses Cambridge and another uses Pearson?
faqs.answer: Yes, and many Dubai schools do exactly this, entering candidates for Cambridge in some subjects and Pearson in others. It is administratively normal and causes no problem for a candidate. What it does cause is a tutoring problem if nobody notices: a tutor working from Cambridge past papers for a subject entered with Pearson will teach good content and the wrong paper technique. Get the code for each subject separately rather than assuming the school uses one board across the whole timetable.

faqs.question: Is a teacher at my child's own school allowed to tutor them privately for IGCSE?
faqs.answer: No. The MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, carries a code of conduct that bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school, and ADEK's professional-ethics rules for Abu Dhabi private and charter school staff prohibit paid private tutoring of students enrolled there. There is also a plain conflict of interest: the person who sets a predicted grade and selects a tier should not also be paid to improve the outcome. An independent specialist on the same syllabus avoids both problems.

faqs.question: My child is in Year 11 and the mocks were poor. Is it too late to start?
faqs.answer: Not too late, but the plan has to change shape. By the spring term of Year 11 the limiting factor is almost never unlearned content; it is paper technique, timing and command-term misreading. So the work becomes past papers from the correct board under timed conditions, marked honestly, with content filled in only where the papers expose a gap. Expect two sessions a week on one or two subjects rather than light cover across five. Mock papers should be read as diagnostics, not predictions.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE subjects do students around Al Qusais struggle with most?
faqs.answer: The pattern in this corridor is consistent: Extended Mathematics, Chemistry and First Language English. Extended maths because multi-step questions punish a single early method error. Chemistry because moles calculations and organic mechanisms carry the top grades and qualitative analysis observations are rarely taught systematically. First Language English because strong speakers often narrate a passage rather than analyse how its language works. All three respond quickly to targeted work, which is why they are the usual first subjects in a plan.

dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-al-qusais.closingHeading: Get the code, then get the tutor
dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-al-qusais.closingBody: The useful first move for an Al Qusais family is an email to the school asking for the syllabus or specification code of every subject your child is entered for. With that list, a tutoring plan narrows fast: the two or three subjects that gate the next step, the tier decisions still open, and the papers that should be on the desk. Tell us the codes, the school and when your child actually gets home, and we will propose a tutor and a trial slot. Lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and if the match is wrong after the trial we will change it.

intro.heading: Find the hour before you find the tutor
paragraphs: Al Rashidiya has better transport than most of the eastern suburbs. There is a Red Line metro station, a major bus interchange, and Dubai Festival City is next door. None of that helps a fifteen-year-old on a school bus. School routes are built to collect efficiently rather than quickly, which means a bus serving Al Rashidiya, Nad Al Hamar and Al Garhoud can put forty minutes between the first child dropped and the last. If your child is at the end of that loop, the front door opens at half past four whatever the school day ended.

Then the airport roads do the rest. Al Rashidiya sits against the approaches to Dubai International, and between four and seven in the evening the surrounding junctions behave accordingly. A parent collecting rather than using the bus faces the same arithmetic from the other direction. Either way the practical result is the same: a 4.30pm tutoring booking is a fiction, and a family who makes one will conclude within a month that tutoring does not work for their child.

What is actually available in most Year 11 households in this area is one reliable weekday hour, usually at six or half past seven, plus a Saturday morning. That is the resource. Everything else on this page is about spending it well: which subject can genuinely use it, how the Dubai academic year interrupts it, how to schedule it when there are two or three children in the house, and how to keep it when Ramadan moves the evening.

On the home-tutoring question, which is the phrase you searched: in-home IGCSE tutoring in Dubai is a real market, priced at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel included, where Bestimate's 2026 rate table gives 180 to 350 and independent tutors advertise 200 to 500. The thing it does not solve is the hour. A tutor driving to Al Rashidiya for a six o'clock booking is in the same traffic the bus was, and the minutes lost at the start of the lesson are not recovered at the end of it.

IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE. Home visiting is a service we run only in India. For an Al Rashidiya family we match a tutor to the exact syllabus code, in the slot you nominate, and teach one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with a free trial lesson in that slot before anything is charged. The reason the format matters here is specific: an online session starts when the clock says so, and it can be moved by message when the school changes something, which in a Dubai term it will.

Nothing here is a claim about grades. What a correctly placed hour changes is how much of the booked time becomes teaching, and how much of that teaching the student is awake enough to absorb. In this area those two factors account for more variation in outcome than the choice between one competent tutor and another, which is why the diary gets the first eight sections of this page.

programmes.name: Key Stage 3

programmes.countryNote: The easiest stage to schedule in this area by a wide margin. A Year 8 student can take a half past five session and still have an evening, and the earlier slots are uncontested because nobody else wants them. It is also the cheapest point at which to fix anything.

programmes.name: Year 10
programmes.description: The first IGCSE year. Full subject load, coursework beginning in some subjects, and tiering decisions being confirmed. Homework rises sharply but the school has not yet started taking evenings for revision clinics, which leaves the diary workable.
programmes.countryNote: The best time to establish a tutoring slot in an Al Rashidiya household, precisely because the competition for the evening has not started. A slot established in Year 10 and kept tends to survive into Year 11; a slot created in Year 11 usually does not.

programmes.name: Year 11
programmes.description: The examination year. Nine or ten subjects, coursework deadlines, mock examinations in the autumn and often again in the spring, plus school revision programmes that occupy weekday afternoons from January onwards. Study leave follows.

programmes.name: The mandatory UAE subjects
programmes.description: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies run in every Dubai private school regardless of the licensed curriculum. KHDA calculates instructional time on a 40-minute lesson unit, advises that any mandatory subject lesson runs at least 25 minutes, and requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies.
programmes.countryNote: The reason a Dubai student's week is fuller than the IGCSE subject count suggests. Families budgeting evenings routinely leave these out, then discover there is no room for the second tutored subject they planned.

dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-al-rashidiya.subjectsIntro: Not every IGCSE subject can use a tutored hour equally well. These are the subjects Al Rashidiya families name, with an honest note on how the hour is best spent in each.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Uses a weekly hour better than almost any other subject, because the work can be set, marked and discussed in a repeating cycle. Best placed earlier in the evening, since new technique does not go in at half past eight.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Needs an alert student, so a six o'clock slot beats a late one. Electricity and waves are the usual targets, and the practical-skills questions can be done later in the evening when new content cannot.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Calculation-heavy areas need early slots; organic families and pattern recognition survive a later one. Worth splitting deliberately if the only available hour is at half past seven.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The most tolerant science of a late slot, because much of the useful work is answer structure and command-term discipline rather than new reasoning. Often the right choice when the only hour is a tired one.

subjects.name: English Language
subjects.description: Works well in a longer weekend block, because directed writing needs planning time inside the session. A weekday hour is better spent reviewing a piece written earlier in the week.

subjects.name: English Literature
subjects.description: Suits a Saturday morning more than a weekday evening. Close reading needs a student with attention left, and a tired fifteen-year-old reading a set text aloud is not learning anything.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Studies
subjects.description: Evaluation technique is drillable in a late slot, which makes these useful subjects to place at half past seven. Case-study work needs more energy and belongs earlier or at the weekend.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Pseudocode and trace tables are mechanical enough to survive a later slot. Any practical programming work should be set between sessions rather than done inside them, which is a better use of the hour anyway.

subjects.name: Geography and History
subjects.description: Content recall is the student's own work and paying by the hour for it is poor value. The hour is better spent on source provenance reasoning, case-study structure and exam-question shape, all of which tolerate a later slot.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.description: Both an IGCSE subject and separately a KHDA-mandated school subject, which are not the same requirement. Scheduling note: this is the subject most often displaced by a tutored hour, and families should check the school's own expectations first.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics
subjects.description: Demanding enough that a late or tired slot is wasted. If the only available hour is at half past eight, this is not the subject to spend it on, and the honest advice is a weekend slot or nothing.

subjects.name: Coordinated or Combined Science
subjects.description: One booking covering three strands needs a diagnosis first, so the hour is spent on the weak strand rather than cycling all three. Otherwise a single weekly hour across three sciences achieves very little.
